planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun to light shade; 'Niagara' blooms on old wood, so prune for shape only right after flowering finishes.

directions: A denser, more compact selection of pearlbush than the species, 'Niagara' forms a tidy rounded mound that smothers itself in pure-white, five-petaled flowers along arching stems in mid-spring, just ahead of most lilacs. Its tighter branching and smaller mature size make it a better fit for foundation plantings and smaller borders than the looser, taller straight species. It tolerates average soils and short dry spells once established but dislikes constantly wet ground. Light shearing right after bloom keeps the habit neat without sacrificing next year's flower display.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root shrubs in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this legume shrub needs no supplemental fertility and resents heavy, poorly drained ground.

directions: This selection replaces the typical broad Caragana leaflet with narrow, thread-like segments that give the whole shrub a soft, airy, fern-like texture quite different from the coarser species. Small yellow pea-flowers open along the branches in mid-spring, followed by narrow seed pods, and as a nitrogen-fixing legume it actually improves the lean, sandy, or alkaline soils where little else will grow. Its extreme cold hardiness and tolerance of wind, drought, and road salt make it a favorite windbreak and screening component on the northern Great Plains. An occasional thinning cut removes old wood and keeps the airy habit from becoming congested.

planting.note: Plant grafted, container-grown standards in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; stake the young graft union until the trunk is sturdy enough to support the cascading crown unaided.

directions: An older, stiffly weeping form of Siberian peashrub, 'Pendula' is almost always grown as a grafted standard, with its cascading branches and ordinary-width compound leaflets forming an umbrella-like crown atop a bare trunk. Small yellow flowers dot the drooping branches in spring, and the coarser leaflets distinguish it at a glance from the finer-textured weeping Caragana cultivars bred more recently. It shares the species' bombproof tolerance for cold, wind, drought, and poor alkaline soil, making it a durable small accent for a rock garden or courtyard where a conventional weeping tree would struggle. Remove any upright shoots that sprout below the graft union so the rootstock doesn't overtake the weeping crown.

planting.note: Plant grafted, container-grown trees in well-drained soil in full sun; this variegated form is distinctly slower and smaller-growing than the straight species and is usually maintained as a specimen rather than a street tree.

directions: This old, uncommon selection of the Japanese pagoda tree carries irregular creamy-white margins and mottling on its compound leaflets, giving the airy, locust-like canopy a lighter, variegated effect through summer. Growth is markedly weaker and more shrubby than the vigorous green-leaved species, so it stays considerably smaller and is best sited as a collector's specimen in an arboretum-style planting rather than a shade tree. Like other pagoda trees it flowers only after reaching maturity, producing sparse creamy-white summer panicles in good years, though the variegated foliage is the main ornamental draw. Grafting onto standard Styphnolobium japonicum rootstock is the reliable way to maintain the variegation, since seedlings do not come true.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs
